passage:
When our tiffin service shut down in my final year, I learned there are many ways people can make you feel worse while trying to help.
My mausi hugged me and said, 'Poor boy, all that effort.' My uncle at a wedding told me I should have done an MBA first, then a business. Someone else mentioned, twice, that my cousin in Pune had just been promoted.
I nodded at all of it. I went home each time feeling smaller.
Hafsa was different. She'd been our first customer. She found me on the library steps a week later and just sat down. 'Tell me what happened,' she said. So I did, all of it, the supplier, the price, the last day. She didn't fix anything. She said, 'That sounds really hard, Nitin.' That was it.
A month later I walked into the placement office for the first time. I think those two hours on the steps are why.

qa.q: Where did Hafsa find Nitin a week after the shutdown?
qa.a: She found him on the library steps.

qa.q: How did Nitin feel after the pity, advice and comparisons from relatives?
qa.a: He felt smaller each time, as if their help pointed out his failure instead of easing it.

qa.q: What did Hafsa's way of helping get right?
qa.a: She listened without judging or fixing, and named how hard it was, which helped Nitin feel steady enough to move forward.

qa.q: How might Nitin's mausi see her own words if she read this account?
qa.a: She might be surprised, since she meant to be kind, and realise that pity made him feel worse rather than supported.

grounding: It shows a young man whose venture failed receiving pity, advice and comparison from relatives, and being helped most by a friend who just listened.

passage:
Counsellor's note, college wellness room. Written by Farida.
Nandini (20) came in on Thursday, two weeks after her CA intermediate results. She said she had failed both groups. She sat with her dupatta twisted round one hand and said she'd come because 'everyone keeps talking at me'.
She listed it quite flatly: her aunt cried and called her 'bechari'; her father forwarded her articles on 'how toppers study'; a neighbour asked, in front of her, whether her cousin had cleared on the first try.
'I know they love me,' she said. 'I just feel like a project now.'
I didn't offer tips. I asked what the last two weeks had been like and let her talk. Near the end she cried, then laughed at herself, and her shoulders dropped.
Next: she has asked to come again next Thursday. I will keep the session for listening unless she asks for planning.

qa.q: How long after her CA intermediate results did Nandini come in?
qa.a: She came in two weeks after her CA intermediate results.

qa.q: What does Nandini mean when she says 'I just feel like a project now'?
qa.a: She feels that her family's pity and advice treat her as something to fix, which leaves her feeling judged rather than loved.

qa.q: Which choice by Farida helped Nandini, and why?
qa.a: Farida gave no tips and let her talk, and that non-judging space let Nandini cry, relax and want to come back.

qa.q: How might Nandini's father see his forwarded articles differently after hearing how she felt?
qa.a: He might understand that his well-meant advice added pressure, and that simply listening could help her more.

grounding: It shows a young woman after a failed exam receiving pity, advice and comparison, and a counsellor whose non-judging listening helps her start to recover.

passage:
The week after I failed the CA intermediate for the second time, our house felt like a waiting room. Chachi brought kheer and a sad face, as if someone had died. Mama phoned with advice: "Switch to MBA, forget CA." At a wedding, an aunty I barely knew asked why I couldn't be like my cousin, who cleared it first attempt. I nodded at everyone and felt smaller each time.
Then my friend Aditi came over on Sunday. She didn't bring kheer or a plan. She sat on the floor of my room, ate chips and said, "Tell me how it actually feels. I won't fix anything."
So I told her. The shame, the anger, the part where I'd started to believe I was the family joke. She just listened. When I finished she said, "That sounds really heavy." That was all.
The next morning I opened my books. I'm Pankaj, and that Sunday is when I started standing up again.

qa.q: What did Chachi bring?
qa.a: Kheer and a sad face.

qa.q: How did Pankaj feel after each comparison and piece of advice?
qa.a: Pankaj felt ashamed and smaller each time, as though failing had turned Pankaj into the family joke.

qa.q: Why did Aditi's visit help more than the advice?
qa.a: She listened without judging or fixing, which let Pankaj say the shame out loud and feel strong enough to open the books again.

qa.q: What might Aditi have been feeling while she just listened?
qa.a: Aditi was likely concerned but calm, holding back the urge to offer solutions so that Pankaj could simply be heard.

grounding: After a failed exam a young adult receives pity, advice and comparison, and a friend's non-judging listening helps them stand up again.

passage:
Mentor's note, college incubator, Friday
Zubin came back to the incubator today for the first time since his food-delivery startup shut down last month. I watched how people met him. One classmate patted his shoulder and said, "So sad, yaar, after all that work." A faculty member gave him a ten-minute talk on what he should have done with pricing. Someone at the coffee machine mentioned that a cousin's company had just raised funds. Zubin kept smiling and nodding, and his tea went cold in his hand.
Then Vijay, his old lab partner, pulled a chair beside him and asked, "Do you want to talk about it, or just sit?" Zubin talked for almost forty minutes. Vijay mostly listened.
On the way out, Zubin stopped at my desk and asked to book the small meeting room next week to think about what's next. I've blocked Tuesday for him.

qa.q: How long did Zubin talk to Vijay?
qa.a: For almost forty minutes.

qa.q: What does Zubin's cold tea suggest about how he felt meeting everyone?
qa.a: He felt uncomfortable and weighed down by the pity, lecture and comparison, smiling politely while hurting inside.

qa.q: What did Vijay do that helped, and what did the mentor add?
qa.a: Vijay offered to listen without judging; the mentor then blocked Tuesday so Zubin could plan his next step.

qa.q: How might Vijay have experienced the conversation?
qa.a: Vijay probably felt that being present mattered more than advising, and was glad to see Zubin open up.

grounding: After his startup fails a young man meets pity, advice and comparison, and a friend's non-judging listening helps him start again.

passage:
Diary, Sunday night
Home for the holidays with three backlogs nobody was supposed to know about. By Friday everyone knew.
Papa's friend told me, "Poor boy, don't worry, not everyone is made for engineering." Pity. Periamma gave me a list of coaching centres. At lunch Anna's name came up four times: he cleared everything, he's in Bengaluru, he sends money home.
I kept eating and saying "Yes, yes." I felt like a dent in the family car.
Tonight Lalitha akka from next door, who I used to do maths with when we were small, called me onto her balcony. She asked, "How are you, really?" and then just waited. I talked about the lab exam where my hands shook. She didn't give me a single tip. When I finished she said, "Thanks for telling me."
First time this week I didn't feel like a problem to be solved.
Harish

qa.q: How many backlogs did Harish have?
qa.a: Three backlogs.

qa.q: How did Harish feel during the family lunch?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and small, like a dent in the family car, as his brother's success kept coming up.

qa.q: Why did Lalitha akka's balcony talk help?
qa.a: She asked how he really was and listened without tips or judgment, so he felt like a person rather than a problem.

qa.q: What might Lalitha akka have understood that the others missed?
qa.a: She seemed to see that Harish needed to be heard more than advised, and was likely glad he trusted her.

grounding: A young man with failed exams receives pity, advice and comparison with his brother, and a neighbour's quiet listening helps him.
